lessonTitle: External Forced Convection: Plates and Cylinders

blocks.text: A cooling fan blows over a hot 20 mm diameter bus bar, and a weather station anemometer wire cools faster in a gale than in a breeze: in both cases the heat loss depends on how the moving fluid thins the layer of fluid next to the surface. Engineers capture that with two dimensionless numbers and one correlation.

blocks.markdown: In **forced convection** an external agent (a fan, pump or the motion of the body itself) drives the flow. Heat leaves a surface into the thin boundary layer of fluid next to it. The heat transfer coefficient $h$ defined by $q=hA(T_s-T_\infty)$ is not a material property; it depends on the flow, the fluid and the geometry, so we correlate it using dimensionless groups.

blocks.title: The key dimensionless numbers
blocks.text:
Reynolds number $Re=VL/
u$ (inertial to viscous forces; $
u$ is the kinematic viscosity in m$^2$/s). Prandtl number $Pr=
u/\alpha=\mu c_p/k$ (momentum to thermal diffusivity). Nusselt number $Nu=hL/k_f$ (convection to conduction in the fluid of conductivity $k_f$). Correlations take the form $Nu=f(Re,Pr)$.

blocks.markdown: Reynolds number decides whether the boundary layer is laminar or turbulent. On a flat plate the transition occurs at about $Re_x\approx5\times10^5$, measured with distance $x$ from the leading edge. Prandtl number decides the relative thickness of the velocity and thermal boundary layers: gases have $Pr\approx0.7$, so the layers are of similar thickness; oils have $Pr\gg1$ and a thin thermal layer inside a thick velocity layer; liquid metals have $Pr\ll1$ and the opposite.

blocks.caption: Average Nusselt number for laminar flow over an isothermal flat plate, properties at the film temperature (T_s + T_inf)/2

blocks.title: Heat loss from a heated flat plate in laminar air flow
blocks.prompt: Air at 20 $^\circ$C flows at 2.0 m/s parallel to a flat plate 0.5 m long (flow direction) and 0.3 m wide, held at 60 $^\circ$C. Use air properties at the film temperature (typical): $k=0.026$ W/m K, $\nu=1.6\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $Pr=0.71$. Find the average heat transfer coefficient and the heat transfer from one face.

steps.text: Reynolds number at the plate end: $Re_L=VL/\nu=2.0\times0.5/(1.6\times10^{-5})=62500$. This is below the transition value of about $5\times10^5$, so the boundary layer is laminar over the whole plate.

blocks.answer: $\overline{Nu}_L\approx148$, $\bar h\approx7.7$ W/m$^2$K and $q\approx46$ W from one face.

blocks.markdown: For flow across a cylinder the boundary layer separates behind the cylinder, so the correlation is empirical. The **Hilpert** form $\overline{Nu}_D=C\,Re_D^mPr^{1/3}$ with the constants below is valid for $Pr\ge0.7$, with $Re_D=VD/\nu$ based on the diameter and properties at the film temperature.

blocks.caption: Hilpert constants for a circular cylinder in cross-flow (gases, $Pr\ge0.7$)

blocks.title: Heat loss from a hot rod in cross-flow
blocks.prompt: Air at 20 $^\circ$C blows at 5.0 m/s across a long horizontal rod of diameter 20 mm whose surface is at 80 $^\circ$C. Use the same typical air properties as before ($k=0.026$ W/m K, $\nu=1.6\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $Pr=0.71$) and the Hilpert correlation $\overline{Nu}_D=C\,Re_D^m Pr^{1/3}$. Find the heat loss per metre.

steps.text: $Re_D=VD/\nu=5.0\times0.020/(1.6\times10^{-5})=6250$. The length scale for a cylinder is its diameter.
This lies in the range $4000<Re_D<40000$, where the table gives $C=0.193$ and $m=0.618$.
Per metre length the area is $\pi D=0.0628$ m$^2$/m, so $q'=\bar h\pi D(T_s-T_\infty)=49.6\times0.0628\times60=187$ W/m.

items: Identify the geometry and pick the length scale: plate length $L$ (flow direction) or cylinder diameter $D$.
Compute $Re$ with fluid properties at the film temperature; decide laminar or turbulent, or the Hilpert range.
Compute $Nu$ from the correlation and check that $Pr$ is within its validity range.

blocks.title: Use the right length and properties
blocks.text: Use $x$ or $L$ in the flow direction for plates and the diameter for cylinders. Take $\nu$, $k$ and $Pr$ at the film temperature, not at $T_\infty$ or $T_s$. The laminar plate formula is invalid if $Re_L>5\times10^5$, since the boundary layer becomes turbulent.

blocks.title: Why dimensionless groups
blocks.text: $Nu$ is the dimensionless heat transfer coefficient. Laminar flow gives $Nu\propto Re^{1/2}$, so $h\propto V^{1/2}$: doubling the speed increases $h$ by 41%, not 100%. $Pr$ enters as $Pr^{1/3}$ because it controls the ratio of boundary layer thicknesses.

points: $Re=VL/\nu$ governs laminar versus turbulent flow (transition near $5\times10^5$ on a flat plate); $Pr=\nu/\alpha$ governs the thermal versus velocity boundary layer thickness.
Cylinder in cross-flow: $\overline{Nu}_D=C\,Re_D^mPr^{1/3}$ with $C,m$ from the $Re_D$ range.
Always state the correlation's validity range and evaluate properties at the film temperature.

questions.stem: The Reynolds number in a convection problem is the ratio of

options.text: convective to conductive heat transfer at the surface
inertial forces to viscous forces in the fluid

questions.correctOptionText: inertial forces to viscous forces in the fluid

distractorRationale.a: This is the inverse of the Reynolds number.
distractorRationale.d: This is the Prandtl number, a fluid property.

questions.explanation: $Re=\rho VL/\mu=VL/\nu$ measures how strongly inertia dominates viscous damping. A large $Re$ means disturbances grow and the boundary layer becomes turbulent.

questions.stem: Liquid metals have $Pr\ll1$. Compared with the velocity boundary layer, the thermal boundary layer in a liquid metal flowing over a plate is

options.text: thicker, because thermal diffusivity is much larger than momentum diffusivity
the same thickness, because $Pr$ only matters for gases
absent, because liquid metals do not conduct heat

questions.correctOptionText: thicker, because thermal diffusivity is much larger than momentum diffusivity

distractorRationale.b: That describes oils ($Pr\gg1$), not liquid metals.
distractorRationale.c: $Pr$ always sets the relative thickness of the two layers.
distractorRationale.d: Liquid metals conduct heat extremely well, which is why $Pr$ is small.

questions.explanation: $Pr=\nu/\alpha$ compares how quickly momentum and heat diffuse. If $\alpha\gg\nu$, heat spreads far beyond the region where velocity has been modified, so the thermal layer is the thicker one.

questions.stem: Air at 20 $^\circ$C flows at 0.8 m/s along a flat plate 1.2 m long in the flow direction. Use $\nu=1.6\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $k=0.026$ W/m K and $Pr=0.71$ (typical film properties). Assuming laminar flow, find the average heat transfer coefficient in W/m$^2$K.
questions.explanation: $Re_L=0.8\times1.2/(1.6\times10^{-5})=60000<5\times10^5$, so the laminar formula applies. $\overline{Nu}_L=0.664\times244.9\times0.8921=145.1$, and $\bar h=\overline{Nu}_Lk/L=145.1\times0.026/1.2=3.14$ W/m$^2$K.

questions.stem: A fine heated wire of diameter 5 mm is held at 70 $^\circ$C in a cross-flow of air at 20 $^\circ$C and 4.0 m/s. Use $\nu=1.6\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $k=0.026$ W/m K and $Pr=0.71$ and the Hilpert correlation. Find the heat loss per metre of wire in W/m.
questions.explanation: $Re_D=4.0\times0.005/(1.6\times10^{-5})=1250$, which falls in the range 40 to 4000 with $C=0.683$, $m=0.466$. So $\overline{Nu}_D=0.683\times1250^{0.466}\times0.8921=16.90$, $\bar h=16.90\times0.026/0.005=87.9$ W/m$^2$K, and $q'=\bar h\pi D\Delta T=69.0$ W/m.

questions.stem: For air with $\nu=1.6\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s flowing at 3.0 m/s over a flat plate, find the distance from the leading edge, in metres, at which the boundary layer would reach the transition value $Re_x=5\times10^5$.
questions.explanation: $Re_x=Vx/\nu$ gives $x_{cr}=5\times10^5\times1.6\times10^{-5}/3.0=2.667$ m. Plates shorter than this are laminar over their whole length, so the laminar average formula can be used.

questions.stem: A plate is in laminar, isothermal parallel flow and the air speed is doubled with everything else unchanged. The average heat transfer coefficient is multiplied by

distractorRationale.a: This would be a linear dependence; laminar plate flow has $Nu\propto Re^{1/2}$.
distractorRationale.c: This assumes $h\propto V^2$, which has no basis.
distractorRationale.d: The exponent 1/3 belongs to $Pr$, not to $Re$.

questions.explanation: With $\overline{Nu}_L\propto Re_L^{1/2}$ and $Re_L\propto V$, $\bar h\propto V^{1/2}$. Doubling $V$ gives a 41% increase, so the heat loss rises less than the speed.

questions.stem: A cylinder in cross-flow has $Re_D=25000$. In the Hilpert correlation table of this lesson, which constants apply?

distractorRationale.a: These are for $40<Re_D<4000$, which is too low.
distractorRationale.b: These are for $40000<Re_D<400000$, which is too high.
distractorRationale.c: These are for $4<Re_D<40$, very low flow.

questions.explanation: $Re_D=25000$ lies between 4000 and 40000, so $C=0.193$ and $m=0.618$ apply. The exponent increases with $Re$ as the flow separates and the wake grows turbulent.

questions.stem: Explain why the heat transfer coefficient correlation for forced convection is written as $Nu=f(Re,Pr)$ and not in terms of velocity, viscosity and conductivity separately. Describe the physical role of each of $Re$ and $Pr$.
markingGuide: Dimensional analysis reduces the many variables ($V$, $L$, $\rho$, $\mu$, $c_p$, $k$) to a few groups, so experiments on one fluid and size apply to others.
$Re=VL/\nu$ measures inertia over viscosity and sets laminar or turbulent boundary layer behaviour and the boundary layer thickness.
$Pr=\nu/\alpha$ compares momentum and thermal diffusion and sets the ratio of velocity to thermal boundary layer thickness.
$Nu=hL/k$ is the dimensionless wall temperature gradient and the output quantity.
questions.explanation: The point of $Nu=f(Re,Pr)$ is similarity: two systems with equal $Re$ and $Pr$ have the same $Nu$. $Re$ controls the flow regime while $Pr$ controls the temperature layer relative to the velocity layer.

questions.stem: For laminar flow over an isothermal flat plate the local Nusselt number is $Nu_x=0.332\,Re_x^{1/2}Pr^{1/3}$. Show that the plate-averaged value is $\overline{Nu}_L=0.664\,Re_L^{1/2}Pr^{1/3}$, and explain physically why $\bar h$ is twice the local value at $x=L$.
markingGuide: Local $h_x=Nu_xk/x\propto x^{-1/2}$ because the boundary layer thickens with $x$.
Physically the leading edge has a very thin boundary layer and large $h$; this raises the average above the local value at the trailing edge.
questions.explanation: Integrating a function that falls as $x^{-1/2}$ gives twice the end value, because the large coefficients near the leading edge are weighted into the average. The result is exact for the laminar similarity solution.

questions.stem: A heated cylinder in cross-flow has diameter $D$. All else (air speed, properties, surface and air temperatures) is the same, but the diameter is doubled, while $Re_D$ stays in the range where $m=0.618$. Find the factor by which the heat loss per metre of cylinder changes, as a dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: With $\overline{Nu}_D\propto Re_D^m\propto D^m$ and $\bar h=\overline{Nu}_Dk/D\propto D^{m-1}$, the heat loss per metre is $q'=\bar h\pi D\Delta T\propto D^{m}$. So the ratio is $2^{0.618}=1.535$. The heat loss rises by about 53%, although $\bar h$ falls by a factor of $2^{-0.382}$.
